svg.aria-label: S3 is the durable store for all three front ends. Two views exist: the live view served by a hub or by local files, which is strongly consistent, and the published view in the bucket, which is a set of RPO-consistent whole-file snapshots. The control namespace holds the cells that make concurrent access safe, and the recovery point differs per front end.
svg.text: The LIVE view — strong, and never in the bucket
a hub's port 2049 and its file API, or a lean workspace's local disk
close-to-open · byte-range locks · atomic rename · no RPO lag
Reads and writes land on the working set, through whatever holds
coherence for it — the hub process, or the agent's own kernel.
Who reads it: front doors, editors, agents — anything touching a
tree that is being changed right now.
The hub's live view offers one thing no real S3 can: assembly under a temp name, completed by an
ATOMIC RENAME under a deny-both OPEN — an atomic, exclusive multipart-complete.
flint-lean has no live view to share at all: its live tree is local disk, visible to exactly one pod.
The PUBLISHED view — the bucket, and the durable copy
RPO-consistent snapshots per subtree, made of untorn whole-file generations
whole objects · versioned · read-only against a live subtree
A reader never sees half a file. It may well see a file from before
your last write — that is the contract, not a defect.
Who reads it: project browsers, DR, analytics, and any non-mount
access — plain S3, with no flint server in the read path at all.
Do not write into a live subtree from the console.
A hand-made PUT under a prefix a hub or syncer owns has three bad fates: overwritten at the next
flush, reported as a conflict, or silently uncited. The bucket is the durable copy, not a second door.
Inside the prefix — the bytes, and the cells that make concurrency safe
Every cell below exists to answer one question that cannot be answered from the object listing alone.
flint-lite writes
<prefix>/<path>
the published generations
.flint/epoch
"who is the hub right now?" — a lease, so a
second hub is fenced instead of interleaved
.flint/manifest
"what is the whole tree?" — DR from one GET
.flint/owner
flint-lean writes
<prefix>/files/<path>
the workspace, file for file
.flint/lean/epoch · claim
"who may write this subtree?" — one holder,
enforced by CAS, across every cluster
.flint/lean/current
"what does the last boundary contain?"
.flint/lean/inbox · conflicts/
flint-passthrough writes
<prefix>/<key>
the objects, and nothing else
There is no control namespace here,
and that is the entire feature.
A prefix owned by somebody else's tooling stays
exactly as it was. flint adds no cells, claims no
lease and leaves no trace when the pod goes away.
You also get no answer to any of the questions on the left.
Reserved, and enforced
`.flint` is control state. A client file under it
can never shadow a control object, and a NESTED
nested/.flint/epoch
is another share's namespace — never tiered into
this one. Both are tested, because both were once
a way to overwrite a live share's lease.
The formats are mutually convertible: a volume can
move between front ends, and DR import is the same
verb in each. Choosing today does not strand data.
What "durable" actually means here — the recovery point, per front end
flint-lite — RPO is the flush cadence
The PVC is a working set the hub flushes on a timer. Losing
the disk is a REBUILD from the bucket, not a loss.
A cold read hydrates on demand and both doors say so rather
than hanging: NFS returns NFS4ERR_DELAY, HTTP returns 503.
Hibernation deletes the PVC, so it is VERIFIED, never assumed:
the operator scales back to one, polls until the hub reports
rpoClean, and only then deletes. A share with no bucket
reports rpoClean: null — which is a refusal, not a pass.
Waking a hibernated share re-imports the whole tree (~79 s).
flint-lean — RPO is the last barrier
A hard pod kill loses at most floorSecs of work (default 60 s).
A graceful stop loses nothing: preStop runs a final barrier.
A container restart over a live tree RESUMES from its baseline
— it does not re-check-out, and does not lose the delta.
Publish at a breakpoint and the RPO becomes zero, knowably:
echo > .flint/publish → .flint/publish.ack = ok
means the bytes are in S3. That is the difference between
"probably durable" and "durable, and I was told so".
Gated mode adds versions; retention must outlast the crash window.
flint-passthrough — there is no RPO
Nothing is buffered on flint's behalf, so nothing can be lost
by flint. A completed PUT is durable the instant S3 says so,
and an interrupted one simply did not happen.
This is the strongest durability story of the three — and it
is strongest because flint is not in it.
The trade is on the other side of the ledger: a write is a
whole new object, there is no rename to make it atomic against
a reader, and two writers racing one key resolve as S3 resolves
them — last writer wins, with nothing recording that a race
occurred, because there is no cell in which to record it.
